section_summary: This section documents Japanese emigration and colonization policy during 1933–1935, especially subsidized settlement in Brazil and armed agricultural settlement in Manchuria. It includes newspaper articles, diplomatic correspondence, internal memoranda, bibliographies, statistical surveys, and two major consular reports examining population pressure, government assistance, migration destinations, and immigration restrictions. Particular attention is given to Brazil’s Couto Amendment, the search for an alternative outlet in Paraguay, and the strategic character and limited demographic value of Japanese settlement in Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the Japanese Settlement at Jiamusi
subfiles.from: G. C. Hanson, American Consul General
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Beijing
subfiles.about: Reports on a subsidized and armed Japanese agricultural settlement at Jiamusi on the lower Songhua River.
subfiles.summary: Hanson forwards an article on the Jiamusi settlement, judging it an expensive small experiment of little military importance beyond a friendly population and bandit protection; Korean settlement is much larger.

subfiles.title: “Armed Migrants”
subfiles.about: Describes the organization, subsidies, living conditions, and intended purpose of the Japanese colony at Jiamusi.
subfiles.summary: Article 'Armed Migrants': only 500 selected men on 40,000 acres near Jiamusi, armed against bandits and given land, tools, allowances and aid; about twenty percent returned; settlement would stay limited and educational.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference Sheet for Despatch No. 646
subfiles.about: Cross-references Ambassador Grew's despatch on the impracticability of colonizing Manchuria and the resulting encouragement of emigration elsewhere.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Despatch 646 with a Chugai Shogyo article recognizing Manchurian colonization's failure and expecting more emigration to South America.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 646: Japanese Immigration to Brazil
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a translated Japanese press article on Japanese immigration to Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Grew calls attention to the article's opening admission that Japanese migration to Manchuria had proved a failure. He suggests that recognition of Manchuria's impracticability as a settlement field would lead Japanese authorities to promote migration to Brazil, South America, and other lands better suited to Japanese ways of life.

subfiles.title: Translated Chugai Shogyo Article on Japanese Emigration
subfiles.about: Reviews the rapid increase of Japanese migration to Brazil after disappointing results in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Translated article: migration to Manchukuo disappointed while movement to Brazil grew rapidly, with 1933 statistics and Brazil's willingness to admit cheap Japanese labor; ending fragmentary.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Betty Turner on Japanese Emigration to South America
subfiles.about: Records advice given to Betty Turner concerning her proposed study of Japanese emigration to Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Betty Turner plans a year in the Far East on Japanese emigration to Latin America; Hornbeck advised cultivating correspondents without close embassy ties; Dooman suggested southern Japan starting with the Kobe consul.

subfiles.title: Betty Turner's Request for Information
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests references and informed contacts for a survey of Japanese emigration worldwide.
subfiles.summary: Turner, studying Japanese migration for a Columbia course, asks for publications or an adviser.

subfiles.title: Department of State Reply to Betty Turner
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Supplies a bibliography and identifies recent statistical sources on Japanese emigration.
subfiles.summary: Department sends Turner a dated bibliography, recommending The Japan Year Book 1931 and the 1933 Résumé Statistique, without responsibility for their statements.

subfiles.title: Bibliography on Japanese Emigration
subfiles.about: Lists English, German, and French works concerning Japanese migration to the United States, the Pacific, and South America.
subfiles.summary: Bibliography of works by Trevor, Ichihashi, Mears, Yoshida, Schultze and Aubert on Japanese residents on the Pacific Coast, causes of emigration, and communities in South America, Hawaii, California and Canada.

subfiles.title: Report No. 7298: Immigration and Emigration
subfiles.about: Surveys the history, organization, geography, statistics, and economic significance of Japanese emigration.
subfiles.summary: The report traces modern Japanese emigration from Hawaii through the exclusionary legislation of the United States and other Anglo-Saxon countries to government-supported settlement in Brazil and Manchuria. It estimates roughly 700,000 Japanese emigrants abroad, describes migration companies and colonization enterprises, and discusses communities throughout Latin America and Southeast Asia. It also records concern over proposed Brazilian restrictions, lists leading prefectures of origin, calculates emigrant remittances, and outlines a Korean plan to send large numbers of families to Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Transmitting a Study to the President
subfiles.about: Transmits a requested memorandum on Japanese immigration to Latin American countries.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum forwards to the President a study prepared at his suggestion, with no analysis.

subfiles.title: Japanese Emigration to Latin American Countries
subfiles.from: J. F. McGurk, Division of Latin American Affairs
subfiles.to: Department of State / President Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese settlement in Latin America, governmental support for emigration, and emerging opposition in Brazil and Peru.
subfiles.summary: McGurk traces Japanese migration from Peru to Brazil and describes the rapid post-1924 expansion of Japanese settlement in São Paulo under subsidies and the supervision of government-backed agencies. He supplies country-by-country population figures and explains Brazil's movement toward constitutional immigration restrictions. The memorandum also reports growing Peruvian hostility toward Japanese commercial competition, manufactured imports, and workers.

subfiles.title: Japanese Emigration to Latin American Countries: Brazil and Peru
subfiles.doc_type: Division of Latin American Affairs memorandum
subfiles.from: J. F. McGurk, Division of Latin American Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese population growth in Brazil and Peru and provides Latin American population figures for 1930.
subfiles.summary: Latin American Affairs memo: Japanese population in Brazil about 147,585 by end of 1933, Brazilian immigration totals 1926 to mid-1933, varying Peru estimates, and a table of Japanese populations where Japan has consuls.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference Sheet for Report No. 143
subfiles.about: Cross-references Report No. 143 on the trend of migratory movement from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Report 143 from Tokyo by Allison, 'Emigration from Japan', answering the June 1, 1934 circular.

subfiles.title: Report No. 143: Trend of Migratory Movement—Japan
subfiles.doc_type: consular research report with statistical appendices
subfiles.from: John Moore Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive historical and statistical analysis of Japanese emigration, immigration, and overseas settlement.
subfiles.summary: Allison traces Japanese emigration from the Meiji period through the growth of government-controlled assisted migration, emphasizing Brazil's rise as the principal destination after exclusion from the United States and other countries. He compares departures with return migration, maps the distribution of Japanese abroad, discusses Korea, Taiwan, the South Seas, and the movement of Korean laborers into Japan, and reviews immigration restrictions. The report concludes that Japanese emigration was government-inspired but demographically insignificant and that industrialization remained Japan's principal answer to population growth. Its appendices supply extensive tables on residence abroad, annual departures and returns, occupation, and age.

subfiles.title: Visa Division Evaluation of “Japanese Emigration in 1934”
subfiles.about: Recommends a high rating for Robert Mills McClintock's report on Japanese emigration in 1934.
subfiles.summary: Visa Division evaluates McClintock's 'Japanese Emigration in 1934': the Couto Amendment, large-scale Brazil migration ended, Manchukuo the only major outlet, trade and shipping to suffer; recommends rating Very Good.

subfiles.title: Japanese Emigration in 1934
subfiles.from: Robert Mills McClintock, American Vice Consul at Kobe; approved by Howard Donovan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the end of large-scale Japanese migration to Brazil and the prospects for settlement in Paraguay and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: McClintock explains how the Couto Amendment reduced Japan's prospective Brazilian quota from about 28,000 migrants to roughly 3,300, although an existing São Paulo contract allowed the record 1934 movement to proceed. He attributes much of that migration to drought, famine, fire, and the collapse of silk farming in several Japanese regions, and assesses the likely loss to Japanese trade, remittances, and Osaka Shosen Kaisha's South American service. Paraguay is considered a possible but uncertain alternative, while the Manchurian colonies are described as armed, heavily subsidized agricultural garrisons directed by the Kwantung Army. The excerpt ends with plans for a government-backed company intended to send 150,000–250,000 Japanese settlers to Manchuria over ten years.
